It’s Greek to Me 
IN THESE LAST THREE CHAPTERS we’ve talked about three sorts of myth: Shakespearean, biblical, and folk/fairy tale. The connection of religion and myth sometimes causes trouble in class when someone takes myth to mean “untrue” and finds it hard to unite that meaning with deeply held religious beliefs. That’s not what I mean by “myth,” though. Rather, what I’m suggesting is the shaping and sustaining power of story and symbol. Whether one believes that the story of Adam and Eve is true, literally or figuratively, matters, but not in this context. Here, in this activity of reading and understanding literature, we’re chiefly concerned with how that story functions as material for literary creators, the way in which it can inform a story or poem, and how it is perceived by the reader. All three of these mythologies work as sources of material, of correspondences, of depth for the modern writer (and every writer is modern—even John Dryden was not archaic when he was writing), and provided they’re recognizable to the reader, they enrich and enhance the reading experience. Of the three, biblical myth probably covers the greatest range of human situations, encompassing all ages of life including the next life, all relationships whether personal or governmental, and all phases of the individual’s experience, physical, sexual, psychological, spiritual. Still, both the worlds of Shakespeare and of fairy and folk tales provide fairly complete coverage as well. 
What we mean in speaking of “myth” in general is story, the ability of story to explain ourselves to ourselves in ways that physics, philosophy, mathematics, chemistry—all very highly useful and informative in their own right—can’t. That explanation takes the shape of stories that are deeply ingrained in our group memory, that shape our culture and are in turn shaped by it, that constitute a way of seeing by which we read the world and, ultimately, ourselves. Let’s say it this way: myth is a body of story that matters. 
Every community has its own body of story that matters. Nineteenth-century composer Richard Wagner went back to the Germanic myths for the material for his operas, and whether the results are good or bad in either historic or musical terms, the impulse to work with his tribal myths is completely understandable. The late twentieth century witnessed a great surge of Native American writing, much of which went back to tribal myth for material, for imagery, for theme, as in the case of Leslie Marmon Silko’s “Yellow Woman,” Louise Erdrich’s Kashpaw/Nanapush novels, and Gerald 
Vizenor’s peculiar Bearheart: The Heirship Chronicles. When Toni Morrison introduces human flight into Song of Solomon, many readers, white readers especially, take her to be referring to Icarus, whereas what she really has in mind, she has said, is the myth of the flying Africans, a story
that matters to her community, her tribe. On one level, there’s not much difference between Silko’s project and Wagner’s; he too is simply going back to the myths of his tribe. We sometimes forget that people in an age of top hats and stiff collars had tribes, but we do so at our peril. In all these cases, what the artist is doing is reaching back for stories that matter to him and his community—for myth. 
In European and Euro-American cultures, of course, there’s another source of myth. Let me rephrase that: MYTH. When most of us think “myth,” we mean the northern shores of the Mediterranean between two and three thousand years ago. We mean Greece and Rome. Greek and Roman myth is so much a part of the fabric of our consciousness, of our unconscious really, that we scarcely notice. You doubt me? In the town where I live, the college teams are known as the Spartans. Our high school? The Trojans. In my state we have a Troy (one of whose high schools is Athens—and they say there are no comedians in education), an Ithaca, a Sparta, a Romulus, a Remus, and a Rome. These communities are scattered around the state and date from different periods of settlement. Now if a town in the center of Michigan, a fair distance from anything that can be called Aegean or Ionian (although it’s not very far from the town of Ionia), can be named Ithaca, it suggests that Greek myth has had pretty good staying power. 
Let’s go back to Toni Morrison for a moment. I’m always slightly amazed that Icarus gets all the ink. It was his father, Daedalus, who crafted the wings, who knew how to get off Crete and safely reach the mainland, and who in fact flew to safety. Icarus, the kid, the daredevil, failed to follow his father’s advice and plunged to his death. His fall remains a source of enduring fascination for us and for our literature and art. In it we see so much: the parental attempt to save the child and the grief at having failed, the cure that proves as deadly as the ailment, the youthful exuberance that leads to self destruction, the clash between sober, adult wisdom and adolescent recklessness, and of course the terror involved in that headlong descent into the sea. Absolutely none of this has anything to do with Morrison and her flying Africans, so it’s little wonder that she’s a bit mystified by this response of her readers. But it’s a story and a pattern that is so deeply burrowed into our consciousness that readers may almost automatically consider it whenever flying or falling is invoked. Clearly it doesn’t fit the situation in Song of Solomon. But it does apply in other works. In 1558 Pieter Brueghel painted a wonderful picture, Landscape with Fall of Icarus. In the foreground we see a plowman and his ox, just beyond him a shepherd and his flock, and at sea a merchant ship sailing placidly along; this is a scene of utter ordinariness and tranquillity. Only in the lower right corner of the painting is there anything even remotely suggestive of trouble: a pair of legs askew as they disappear into the water. That’s our boy. He really doesn’t have much of a presence in the frame, but his presence makes all the difference. Without the pathos of the doomed boy, we have a picture of farming and merchant shipping with no narrative or thematic power. I teach, with some regularity, two great poems based on that painting, W. H. Auden’s “Musée des Beaux Arts” (1940) and William Carlos Williams’s 
“Landscape with Fall of Icarus” (1962). They’re wonderful poems, very different from each other in tone, style, and form, but in essential agreement about how the world goes on even in the face of our private tragedies. Each artist alters what he finds in the painting. Brueghel introduces the plowman and the ship, neither of which appears in the version that comes to us from the Greeks. And Williams and Auden find, in their turn, slightly different elements to emphasize in the painting. Williams’s
poem stresses the pictorial elements of the painting, trying to capture the scene while sneaking in the thematic elements. Even his arrangement of the poem on the page, narrow and highly vertical, recalls the body plummeting from the sky. Auden’s poem, on the other hand, is a meditation on the private nature of suffering and the way in which the larger world takes no interest in our private disasters. It is astonishing and pleasing to discover that the painting can occasion these two very different responses. Beyond them, readers find their own messages in all this. As someone who was a teenager in the sixties, I am reminded by the fate of Icarus of all those kids who bought muscle cars with names like Mustang and Firebird and Charger and Barracuda. All the driver education and solid parental advice in the world can’t overcome the allure of that kind of power, and sadly, in too many cases those young drivers shared the fate of Icarus. My students, somewhat younger than I am, will inevitably draw other parallels. Still, it all goes back to the myth: the boy, the wings, the unscheduled dive. 
So that’s one way classical myth can work: overt subject matter for poems and paintings and operas and novels. What else can myth do? 
Here’s a thought. Let’s say you wanted to write an epic poem about a community of poor fishermen in the Caribbean. If this was a place you came from, and you knew these people like you know your own family, you’d want to depict the jealousies and resentments and adventure and danger, as well as capturing their dignity and their life in a way that conveys all that has escaped the notice of tourists and white property owners. You could, I suppose, try being really, really earnest, portraying the characters as very serious and sober, making them noble by virtue of their goodness. But I bet that wouldn’t work. What you’d wind up with instead would probably be very stiff and artificial, and artificiality is never noble. Besides, these folks aren’t saints. They make a lot of mistakes: they’re petty, envious, lustful, occasionally greedy as well as courageous, elegant, powerful, knowledgeable, profound. And you want noble, after all, not Tonto—there’s no Lone Ranger here. Alternatively, you might try grafting their story onto some older story of rivalry and violence, a story where even the victor is ultimately doomed, a story where, despite occasional personal shortcomings, the characters have an unmistakable nobility. You could give your characters names like Helen, Philoctetes, Hector, and Achille. At least that’s what Nobel Prize winner Derek Walcott does in his Omeros (1990). Those names are drawn, of course, from The Iliad, although Walcott uses elements—parallels, persons, and situations—of both it and The Odyssey in his epic. 
The question we will inevitably ask is, Why? 
Why should someone in the late twentieth century draw on a story that was passed along orally from the twelfth through the eighth century b.c. and not written down until maybe two or three hundred years later? Why should someone try to compare modern fishermen with these legendary heroes, many of whom were descended from gods? Well for starters, Homer’s legendary heroes were farmers and fishermen. Besides, aren’t we all descended from gods? Walcott reminds us by this parallel of the potential for greatness that resides in all of us, no matter how humble our worldly circumstances. 
That’s one answer. The other is that the situations match up more closely than we might expect. The plot of The Iliad is not particularly divine or global. Those who have never read it assume mistakenly that it is the story of the Trojan War. It is not. It is the story of a single, rather lengthy action: the wrath
of Achilles (a mere fifty-three days out of ten years). Achilles becomes angry with his leader, Agamemnon, withdraws his support from the Greeks, only rejoining the battle when the consequences of his action have destroyed his best friend, Patroclus. At this point he turns his wrath against the Trojans and in particular their greatest hero, Hector, whom he eventually kills. His reason for such anger? Agamemnon has taken his war prize. Trivial? It gets worse. The prize is a woman. Agamemnon, forced by divine order and by public sentiment to return his concubine to her father, retaliates against the person who most publicly sided against him, Achilles, by taking his concubine, Briseis. Is that petty enough? Is that noble? No Helen, no judgment of Paris, no Trojan horse. At its core, it’s the story of a man who goes berserk because his stolen war bride is confiscated, acted out against a background of wholesale slaughter, the whole of which is taking place because another man, Menelaus (brother of Agamemnon) has had his wife stolen by Paris, half brother of Hector. That’s how Hector winds up having to carry the hopes for salvation of all Troy on his shoulders. 
And yet somehow, through the centuries, this story dominated by the theft of two women has come to epitomize ideals of heroism and loyalty, sacrifice and loss. Hector is more stubbornly heroic in his doomed enterprise than anyone you’ve ever seen. Achilles’ grief at the loss of his beloved friend is truly heartbreaking. The big duels—between Hector and Ajax, between Diomedes and Paris, between Hector and Patroclus, between Hector and Achilles—are genuinely exciting and suspenseful, their outcomes sources of grand celebration and dismay. No wonder so many modern writers have often borrowed from and emulated Homer. 
And when did that begin? 
Almost immediately. Virgil, who died in 19 b.c., patterned his Aeneas on the Homeric heroes. If Achilles did it or Odysseus went there, so does Aeneas. Why? It’s what heroes do. Aeneas goes to the underworld. Why? Odysseus went there. He kills a giant from the enemy camp in a final climactic battle. Why? Achilles did. And so on. The whole thing is less derivative than it sounds and not without humor and irony. Aeneas and his followers are survivors of Troy, so here we have this Trojan hero acting out the patterns set down by his enemies. Moreover, when these Trojans sail past Ithaca, home to Odysseus, they jeer and curse the agent of their destruction. On the whole, though, Virgil has him undertake these actions because Homer had already defined what it means to be a hero. 
Back to Walcott. Almost exactly two thousand years after Virgil, Walcott has his heroes perform actions that we can recognize as symbolic reenactments of those in Homer. Sometimes it’s a bit of a stretch, since we can’t have a lot of battlefield duels out in the fishing boats. Nor can he call his Helen “the face that launched a thousand dinghies.” Lacks grandeur, that phrase. What he can do, though, is place them in situations where their nobility and their courage are put to the test, while reminding us that they are acting out some of the most basic, most primal patterns known to humans, exactly as Homer did all those centuries before. The need to protect one’s family: Hector. The need to maintain one’s dignity: Achilles. The determination to remain faithful and to have faith: Penelope. The struggle to return home: Odysseus. Homer gives us four great struggles of the human being: with nature, with the divine, with other humans, and with ourselves. What is there, after all, against which we need to prove ourselves but those four things? 
In our modern world, of course, parallels may be ironized, that is, turned on their head for
purposes of irony. How many of us would see the comedy of three escaped convicts as parallel to the wanderings of Odysseus? Still, that’s what brothers Joel and Ethan Coen give us in their 2000 film O Brother, Where Art Thou? It’s about trying to get home, isn’t it? Or this, the most famous example: a single day in Dublin in 1904, on which a young man decides on his future and an older man wanders the city, eventually returning home to his wife in the small hours of the next morning. The book has only one overt clue that this all might have something to do with Homer, its one-word title: Ulysses (1922). As we now know, James Joyce envisioned every one of the eighteen episodes of the novel as a parallel to some incident or situation in The Odyssey. There’s an episode in a newspaper office, for instance, which parallels Odysseus’s visit to Aeolus, the god of the winds, but the parallel may seem pretty tenuous. To be sure, newspapermen are a windy group and there are a lot of rhetorical flourishes in the episode, to say nothing of the fact that a gust of wind does zip through at one point. Still, we can see it as resembling the Homeric original only if we understand that resemblance in terms of a funhouse mirror, full of distortion and goofy correspondences—if we understand it, in other words, as an ironic parallel. The fact that it’s ironic makes the parallel—and the Aeolus episode—such fun. Joyce is less interested than Walcott in investing his characters with classical nobility, although finally they do take on something of that quality. After watching poor old Leopold Bloom stroll around Dublin all day and half the night, running into no end of trouble and recalling great heartbreak in his life, we may well come to feel he is noble in his own way. His nobility, however, is not that of Odysseus. 
Greek and Roman myth, of course, is more than Homer. The transformations of Ovid’s Metamorphoses show up in all sorts of later works, not least in Franz Kafka’s story of a man who wakes up one morning to find he’s changed into an enormous beetle. چرا کسی در اواخر سده بیستم باید به داستانی رجوع کند که به صورت شفاهی از سده دوازدهم تا هشتم پیش از میلاد منتقل شده و شاید تا دویست یا سیصد سال بعد مکتوب نشده است؟ چرا کسی باید سعی کند ماهیگیران مدرن را با این قهرمانان افسانه‌ای مقایسه کند، که بسیاری از آنها از نسل خدایان بودند؟ خوب، برای شروع، قهرمانان افسانه‌ای هومر کشاورز و ماهیگیر بودند. گذشته از این، مگر نه اینکه همه ما از نسل خدایانیم؟ والکات با این هم‌نشینی به ما یادآوری می‌کند که پتانسیل عظمت در همه ما وجود دارد، صرف‌نظر از اینکه شرایط دنیوی‌ چقدر فروتنانه باشد.  

این یک پاسخ است. پاسخ دیگر این است که موقعیت‌ها بیش از آنچه انتظار داریم با هم مطابقت دارند. طرح ایلیاد چندان الهی یا جهانی نیست. کسانی که هرگز آن را نخوانده‌اند به اشتباه گمان می‌برند که داستان جنگ تروا است. نیست. داستان یک کنش واحد و نسبتاً طولانی است: خشم آشیل (فقط پنجاه‌و‌سه روز از ده سال). آشیل بر رهبرش، آگاممنون، خشم می‌گیرد، پشتیبانی خود را از یونانیان پس می‌گیرد، و تنها زمانی به نبرد بازمی‌گردد که پیامدهای عملش بهترین دوستش، پاتروکلوس، را نابود کرده است. در این نقطه خشم خود را متوجه تروایی‌ها و به‌ویژه بزرگترین قهرمانشان، هکتور، می‌کند که در نهایت او را می‌کشد. دلیل چنین خشم‌اش؟ آگاممنون غنیمت جنگی‌اش را گرفته است. پیش‌پاافتاده؟ بدتر می‌شود. غنیمت یک زن است. آگاممنون، که به دستور الهی و احساسات عمومی مجبور به بازگرداندن معشوقه‌اش به پدرش می‌شود، علیه کسی که آشکارترین مخالفت را با او کرده بود، آشیل، با گرفتن معشوقه‌اش، بریسئیس، تلافی می‌کند. به اندازه کافی خرده‌بینانه است؟ نجیبانه است؟ هیچ هلنی، هیچ داوری پاریس، هیچ اسب تروا. در هسته خود، داستان مردی است که به خاطر مصادره عروس جنگی دزدیده‌شده‌اش خشمگین می‌شود، که در پس‌ای از کشتار گسترده اجرا می‌شود، که کل آن به این دلیل رخ می‌دهد که مرد دیگری، منلائوس (برادر آگاممنون)، همسرش توسط پاریس، برادر ناتنی هکتور، دزدیده شده است. اینگونه است که هکتور ناگزیر می‌شود امیدهای نجات کل تروا را بر دوش بکشد.  

و با این حال به نحوی، در طول سده‌ها، این داستان که با دزدی دو زن تسخیر شده، به تجسم ایده‌آل‌های قهرمانی و وفاداری، فداکاری و ازدست‌دادن بدل شده است. هکتور در کار محکوم‌به‌شکستش سرسختانه‌تر از هر کسی که دیده‌اید قهرمان است. اندوه آشیل بر ازدست‌دادن دوست محبوبش واقعاً دل‌اشک‌بار است. دوئل‌های بزرگ – بین هکتور و آژاکس، بین دیومدس و پاریس، بین هکتور و پاتروکلوس، بین هکتور و آشیل – به‌راستی هیجان‌انگیز و پرتعلیق هستند، و پیامدهایشان منبعی از جشن‌و‌شادی و ناامیدی بزرگ. جای شگفتی نیست که بسیاری از نویسندگان مدرن اغلب از هومر وام گرفته‌اند و از او تقلید کرده‌اند.  

و این چه زمانی آغاز شد؟  

تقریباً بلافاصله. ویرژیل، که در ۱۹ پیش از میلاد درگذشت، آینیاس خود را بر اساس قهرمانان هومری الگوبرداری کرد. اگر آشیل کاری کرد یا اودیسه جایی رفت، آینیاس هم می‌کند. چرا؟ این کاری است که قهرمانان می‌کنند. آینیاس به جهان اموات می‌رود. چرا؟ اودیسه رفت. او در نبرد اوج نهایی غولی از اردوگاه دشمن را می‌کشد. چرا؟ آشیل این کار را کرد. و الی آخر. کل ماجرا کمتر از آنچه به نظر می‌رسد اقتباسی است و خالی از طنز و کنایه نیست. آینیاس و پیروانش بازماندگان تروا هستند، پس در اینجا این قهرمان تروایی داریم که الگوهای تعیین‌شده توسط دشمنانش را اجرا می‌کند. افزون بر این، وقتی این تروایی‌ها از کنار ایتاکا، خانه اودیسه، می‌گذرند، به عامل نابودی‌شان ناسزا می‌گویند و لعن‌ش می‌کنند. اما به‌طور کلی، ویرژیل او را به این کنش‌ها وامیدارد زیرا هومر پیش‌تر تعریف کرده بود که قهرمان بودن چه معنایی دارد.  

بازگردیم به والکات. تقریباً دقیقاً دو هزار سال پس از ویرژیل، والکات قهرمانانش را به انجام کنش‌هایی واداشته که می‌توانیم به عنوان بازاجرایی نمادین کنش‌های هومر تشخیص دهیم. گاه کمی کشش دارد، چون نمی‌توانیم دوئل‌های زیادی در میدان نبرد در قایق‌های ماهیگیری داشته باشیم. و نه می‌تواند هلنش را «چهره‌ای که هزار قایق پارویی را به آب انداخت» بنامد. آن عبارت شکوه ندارد. اما آنچه می‌تواند بکند، قرار دادن آنها در موقعیت‌هایی است که نجابت و شجاعت‌ محک می‌خورد، در حالی که به ما یادآوری می‌کند که آنها برخی از بنیادی‌ترین و اصیل‌ترین الگوهای شناخته‌شده برای انسان را اجرا می‌کنند، دقیقاً همانطور که هومر قرن‌ها پیش انجام داد. نیاز به محافظت از خانواده: هکتور. نیاز به حفظ شأن: آشیل. عزم به وفادار ماندن و وفاداری داشتن: پنلوپه. تلاش برای بازگشت به خانه: اودیسه. هومر چهار مبارزه بزرگ انسان را به ما می‌دهد: با طبیعت، با امر الوهی، با دیگر انسان‌ها و با خودمان. در نهایت، چه چیزی وجود دارد که نیاز داشته باشیم خود را در برابر آن ثابت کنیم جز این چهار چیز؟  

البته در جهان مدرن ما، هم‌نشینی‌ها ممکن است آیرونایز (ironized) شوند، یعنی برای مقاصد کنایه‌ای وارونه شوند. چند نفر از ما کمدی سه زند فراری را موازی با سرگردانی‌های اودیسه می‌بینیم؟ با این حال، این همان چیزی است که برادران جوئل و ایتان کوئن در فیلم ۲۰۰۰ خود «ای برادر، کجایی؟» به ما ارائه می‌دهند. این درباره تلاش برای رسیدن به خانه است، نیست؟ یا این، مشهورترین مثال: یک روز واحد در دوبلین در سال ۱۹۰۴، که در آن مردی جوان درباره آینده‌اش تصمیم می‌گیرد و مردی مسن‌تر در شهر سرگردان است، و در نهایت سحرگاه روز بعد به خانه نزد همسرش بازمی‌گردد. کتاب تنها یک سرنخ آشکار دارد که همه اینها ممکن است ربطی به هومر داشته باشد، عنوان تک‌واژه‌اش: اولیس (۱۹۲۲). همانطور که اکنون می‌دانیم، جیمز جویس هر یک از هجده اپیزود رمان را موازی با حادثه‌ای یا موقعیتی در ادیسه تصور کرد. برای مثال، اپیزودی در دفتر روزنامه وجود دارد که موازی با دیدار اودیسه از آیولوس، خدای بادهاست، اما این هم‌نشینی ممکن است بسیار سست به نظر برسد. مسلماً، روزنامه‌نگاران گروهی پرگو هستند و در این اپیزود جلوه‌های بلاغی زیادی وجود دارد، گذشته از این واقعیت که نسیمی در یک نقطه با سرعت می‌وزد. با این حال، تنها در صورتی می‌توانیم آن را شبیه به اصل هومری ببینیم که این شباهت را در آینه‌های کج‌و‌معوج خانه‌های سرگرمی بفهمیم، پر از تحریف و هم‌نشینی‌های مسخره – به عبارت دیگر، اگر آن را به عنوان هم‌نشینی کنایه‌ای بفهمیم. این واقعیت که کنایه‌ای است، هم‌نشینی – و اپیزود آیولوس – را چنین لذت‌بخش می‌کند. جویس کمتر از والکات علاقه‌مند است که به شخصیت‌�هایش نجابت کلاسیک ببخشد، هرچند در نهایت آنها چیزی از آن کیفیت را به خود می‌گیرند. پس از تماشای لئوپولد بلومِ بی‌چاره که تمام روز و نیمی از شب در دوبلین پرسه می‌زند، با بی‌پایان دردسر مواجه می‌شود و اندوه‌های بزرگ زندگی‌اش را به یاد می‌آورد، به خوبی ممکن است احساس کنیم که او به شیوه خود نجیب است. اما نجابت او، نجابت اودیسه نیست.  

اسطوره یونانی و رومی، البته، فراتر از هومر است. دگردیسی‌های «دگردیسی‌ها» اثر اووید در انواع آثار بعدی ظاهر می‌شوند، به‌ویژه در داستان فرانتس کافکا درباره مردی که یک صبح بیدار می‌شود و می‌بیند به سوسک غول‌پیکری تبدیل شده است. او آن را «مسخ» نامید. ایندیانا جونز ممکن است کاملاً هالیوودی به نظر برسد، اما جستجوگر بی‌باک گنج‌های افسانه‌ای به آپولونیوس و «آرگوناتیکا»، داستان جیسون و آرگونات‌ها، بازمی‌گردد. چیزی کمی خودمانی‌تر؟ نمایش‌های سوفوکل درباره ادیپ و خاندان محکوم‌به‌نابودی‌اش بارها و بارها در انواع واریاسیون‌ها ظاهر می‌شوند. در واقع، هیچ شکلی از خانواده ناکارآمد یا هیچ فروپاشی شخصیتی فردی وجود ندارد که مدل یونانی یا رومی برای آن وجود نداشته باشد. بی‌جهت نیست که نام شخصیت‌های تراژیک یونانی در نظریه‌های فروید ظاهر می‌شوند. زن بی‌عدالتی‌دیده که در اندوه و جنونش خشن شده است؟ آیا آینیاس و دیدو را می‌خواهید یا جیسون و مدیا؟ و مانند هر دین اولیه خوبی، توضیحی برای پدیده‌های طبیعی داشتند، از تغییر فصل‌ها (دمتر و پرسفونه و هادس) تا اینکه چرا بلبل صدایش آنگونه است (فیلومنا و تریوس). خوشبختانه برای ما، بیشتر آن مکتوب شد، اغلب در چندین نسخه، تا به این ساختار روایی شگفت‌انگیز دسترسی داشته باشیم. و چون نویسندگان و خوانندگان دانش بخش بزرگی از این ساختار روایی، این اسطوره‌شناسی، را به اشتراک می‌گذارند، وقتی نویسندگان از آن استفاده می‌کنند، ما خوانندگان آن را تشخیص می‌دهیم، گاه به طور کامل، گاه فقط مبهم یا فقط به این دلیل که نسخه لونی تونز (Looney Tunes) را می‌شناسیم. این تشخیص تجربه ما از ادبیات را غنی‌تر، عمیق‌تر، معنادارتر می‌سازد، به‌طوری که داستان‌های مدرن خودمان نیز اهمیت می‌یابند و در قدرت اسطوره شریک می‌شوند.  

از میان جالب‌ترین تحولات اخیر در نوشتن برای خوانندگان جوان، مجموعه «پرسی جکسون و المپنشین‌ها» اثر ریک ریوردن است. پنج‌گانه رمان‌ها با «دزد صاعقه» (۲۰۰۵) آغاز می‌شود. پرسی نوجوانی است که نمی‌تواند جایی برای خود پیدا کند و می‌فهمد پسر پوزیدون است و متهم به دزدیدن سلاح برگزیده زئوس، صاعقه، شده است. سپس می‌فهمد دوستش ساتیر است، با مینوتور می‌جنگد، با دختری از آتنا دوست می‌شود، و همه جهنم به پا می‌شود. به عنوان یک نیمه‌خدا، پرسی با عادی‌بودن مشکل دارد (چیزهایی مانند ADHD و دیسلکسیا)، اما در جبهه قهرمانی واقعی است، همانطور که بارها و بارها فرصت اثباتش را می‌یابد. تبار الهی‌اش کمک می‌کند، همانطور که دوستان اسطوره‌ای‌اش. یک چیز است، می‌دانید، فرزند شاگرد ستاره‌دار سابق در مدرسه آمادگی جادوگری‌تان باشید، اما خدای دریا را پدر داشته باشید، خب...  

آه، فراموش کردم بگویم؟ آن عنوان والکات، «اومروس»؟ در گویش محلی، به معنای هومر است. طبیعتاً.

Here, in this activity of reading and understanding literature, we’re chiefly concerned with how that story functions as material for literary creators, the way in which it can inform a story or poem, and how it is perceived by the reader. All three of these mythologies work as sources of material, of correspondences, of depth for the modern writer (and every writer is modern—even John Dryden was not archaic when he was writing), and provided they’re recognizable to the reader, they enrich and enhance the reading experience. Of the three, biblical myth probably covers the greatest range of human situations, encompassing all ages of life including the next life, all relationships whether personal or governmental, and all phases of the individual’s experience, physical, sexual, psychological, spiritual. Still, both the worlds of Shakespeare and of fairy and folk tales provide fairly complete coverage as well. 
What we mean in speaking of “myth” in general is story, the ability of story to explain ourselves to ourselves in ways that physics, philosophy, mathematics, chemistry—all very highly useful and informative in their own right—can’t. That explanation takes the shape of stories that are deeply ingrained in our group memory, that shape our culture and are in turn shaped by it, that constitute a way of seeing by which we read the world and, ultimately, ourselves. Let’s say it this way: myth is a body of story that matters. 
Every community has its own body of story that matters. Nineteenth-century composer Richard Wagner went back to the Germanic myths for the material for his operas, and whether the results are good or bad in either historic or musical terms, the impulse to work with his tribal myths is completely understandable. The late twentieth century witnessed a great surge of Native American writing, much of which went back to tribal myth for material, for imagery, for theme, as in the case of Leslie Marmon Silko’s “Yellow Woman,” Louise Erdrich’s Kashpaw/Nanapush novels, and Gerald 
Vizenor’s peculiar Bearheart: The Heirship Chronicles. When Toni Morrison introduces human flight into Song of Solomon, many readers, white readers especially, take her to be referring to Icarus, whereas what she really has in mind, she has said, is the myth of the flying Africans, a story
that matters to her community, her tribe. On one level, there’s not much difference between Silko’s project and Wagner’s; he too is simply going back to the myths of his tribe. We sometimes forget that people in an age of top hats and stiff collars had tribes, but we do so at our peril. In all these cases, what the artist is doing is reaching back for stories that matter to him and his community—for myth. 
In European and Euro-American cultures, of course, there’s another source of myth. Let me rephrase that: MYTH. When most of us think “myth,” we mean the northern shores of the Mediterranean between two and three thousand years ago. We mean Greece and Rome. Greek and Roman myth is so much a part of the fabric of our consciousness, of our unconscious really, that we scarcely notice. You doubt me? In the town where I live, the college teams are known as the Spartans. Our high school? The Trojans. In my state we have a Troy (one of whose high schools is Athens—and they say there are no comedians in education), an Ithaca, a Sparta, a Romulus, a Remus, and a Rome. These communities are scattered around the state and date from different periods of settlement. Now if a town in the center of Michigan, a fair distance from anything that can be called Aegean or Ionian (although it’s not very far from the town of Ionia), can be named Ithaca, it suggests that Greek myth has had pretty good staying power. 
Let’s go back to Toni Morrison for a moment. I’m always slightly amazed that Icarus gets all the ink. It was his father, Daedalus, who crafted the wings, who knew how to get off Crete and safely reach the mainland, and who in fact flew to safety. Icarus, the kid, the daredevil, failed to follow his father’s advice and plunged to his death. His fall remains a source of enduring fascination for us and for our literature and art. In it we see so much: the parental attempt to save the child and the grief at having failed, the cure that proves as deadly as the ailment, the youthful exuberance that leads to self destruction, the clash between sober, adult wisdom and adolescent recklessness, and of course the terror involved in that headlong descent into the sea. Absolutely none of this has anything to do with Morrison and her flying Africans, so it’s little wonder that she’s a bit mystified by this response of her readers. But it’s a story and a pattern that is so deeply burrowed into our consciousness that readers may almost automatically consider it whenever flying or falling is invoked. Clearly it doesn’t fit the situation in Song of Solomon. But it does apply in other works. In 1558 Pieter Brueghel painted a wonderful picture, Landscape with Fall of Icarus. In the foreground we see a plowman and his ox, just beyond him a shepherd and his flock, and at sea a merchant ship sailing placidly along; this is a scene of utter ordinariness and tranquillity. Only in the lower right corner of the painting is there anything even remotely suggestive of trouble: a pair of legs askew as they disappear into the water. That’s our boy. He really doesn’t have much of a presence in the frame, but his presence makes all the difference. Without the pathos of the doomed boy, we have a picture of farming and merchant shipping with no narrative or thematic power. I teach, with some regularity, two great poems based on that painting, W. H. Auden’s “Musée des Beaux Arts” (1940) and William Carlos Williams’s 
“Landscape with Fall of Icarus” (1962). They’re wonderful poems, very different from each other in tone, style, and form, but in essential agreement about how the world goes on even in the face of our private tragedies. Each artist alters what he finds in the painting. Brueghel introduces the plowman and the ship, neither of which appears in the version that comes to us from the Greeks. And Williams and Auden find, in their turn, slightly different elements to emphasize in the painting. Williams’s
poem stresses the pictorial elements of the painting, trying to capture the scene while sneaking in the thematic elements. Even his arrangement of the poem on the page, narrow and highly vertical, recalls the body plummeting from the sky. Auden’s poem, on the other hand, is a meditation on the private nature of suffering and the way in which the larger world takes no interest in our private disasters. It is astonishing and pleasing to discover that the painting can occasion these two very different responses. Beyond them, readers find their own messages in all this. As someone who was a teenager in the sixties, I am reminded by the fate of Icarus of all those kids who bought muscle cars with names like Mustang and Firebird and Charger and Barracuda. All the driver education and solid parental advice in the world can’t overcome the allure of that kind of power, and sadly, in too many cases those young drivers shared the fate of Icarus. My students, somewhat younger than I am, will inevitably draw other parallels. Still, it all goes back to the myth: the boy, the wings, the unscheduled dive. 
So that’s one way classical myth can work: overt subject matter for poems and paintings and operas and novels. What else can myth do? 
Here’s a thought. Let’s say you wanted to write an epic poem about a community of poor fishermen in the Caribbean. If this was a place you came from, and you knew these people like you know your own family, you’d want to depict the jealousies and resentments and adventure and danger, as well as capturing their dignity and their life in a way that conveys all that has escaped the notice of tourists and white property owners. You could, I suppose, try being really, really earnest, portraying the characters as very serious and sober, making them noble by virtue of their goodness. But I bet that wouldn’t work. What you’d wind up with instead would probably be very stiff and artificial, and artificiality is never noble. Besides, these folks aren’t saints. They make a lot of mistakes: they’re petty, envious, lustful, occasionally greedy as well as courageous, elegant, powerful, knowledgeable, profound. And you want noble, after all, not Tonto—there’s no Lone Ranger here. Alternatively, you might try grafting their story onto some older story of rivalry and violence, a story where even the victor is ultimately doomed, a story where, despite occasional personal shortcomings, the characters have an unmistakable nobility. You could give your characters names like Helen, Philoctetes, Hector, and Achille. At least that’s what Nobel Prize winner Derek Walcott does in his Omeros (1990). Those names are drawn, of course, from The Iliad, although Walcott uses elements—parallels, persons, and situations—of both it and The Odyssey in his epic. 
The question we will inevitably ask is, Why? 
Why should someone in the late twentieth century draw on a story that was passed along orally from the twelfth through the eighth century b.c. and not written down until maybe two or three hundred years later? Why should someone try to compare modern fishermen with these legendary heroes, many of whom were descended from gods? Well for starters, Homer’s legendary heroes were farmers and fishermen. Besides, aren’t we all descended from gods? Walcott reminds us by this parallel of the potential for greatness that resides in all of us, no matter how humble our worldly circumstances. 
That’s one answer. The other is that the situations match up more closely than we might expect. The plot of The Iliad is not particularly divine or global. Those who have never read it assume mistakenly that it is the story of the Trojan War. It is not. It is the story of a single, rather lengthy action: the wrath
of Achilles (a mere fifty-three days out of ten years). Achilles becomes angry with his leader, Agamemnon, withdraws his support from the Greeks, only rejoining the battle when the consequences of his action have destroyed his best friend, Patroclus. At this point he turns his wrath against the Trojans and in particular their greatest hero, Hector, whom he eventually kills. His reason for such anger? Agamemnon has taken his war prize. Trivial? It gets worse. The prize is a woman. Agamemnon, forced by divine order and by public sentiment to return his concubine to her father, retaliates against the person who most publicly sided against him, Achilles, by taking his concubine, Briseis. Is that petty enough? Is that noble? No Helen, no judgment of Paris, no Trojan horse. At its core, it’s the story of a man who goes berserk because his stolen war bride is confiscated, acted out against a background of wholesale slaughter, the whole of which is taking place because another man, Menelaus (brother of Agamemnon) has had his wife stolen by Paris, half brother of Hector. That’s how Hector winds up having to carry the hopes for salvation of all Troy on his shoulders. 
And yet somehow, through the centuries, this story dominated by the theft of two women has come to epitomize ideals of heroism and loyalty, sacrifice and loss. Hector is more stubbornly heroic in his doomed enterprise than anyone you’ve ever seen. Achilles’ grief at the loss of his beloved friend is truly heartbreaking. The big duels—between Hector and Ajax, between Diomedes and Paris, between Hector and Patroclus, between Hector and Achilles—are genuinely exciting and suspenseful, their outcomes sources of grand celebration and dismay. No wonder so many modern writers have often borrowed from and emulated Homer. 
And when did that begin? 
Almost immediately. Virgil, who died in 19 b.c., patterned his Aeneas on the Homeric heroes. If Achilles did it or Odysseus went there, so does Aeneas. Why? It’s what heroes do. Aeneas goes to the underworld. Why? Odysseus went there. He kills a giant from the enemy camp in a final climactic battle. Why? Achilles did. And so on. The whole thing is less derivative than it sounds and not without humor and irony. Aeneas and his followers are survivors of Troy, so here we have this Trojan hero acting out the patterns set down by his enemies. Moreover, when these Trojans sail past Ithaca, home to Odysseus, they jeer and curse the agent of their destruction. On the whole, though, Virgil has him undertake these actions because Homer had already defined what it means to be a hero. 
Back to Walcott. Almost exactly two thousand years after Virgil, Walcott has his heroes perform actions that we can recognize as symbolic reenactments of those in Homer. Sometimes it’s a bit of a stretch, since we can’t have a lot of battlefield duels out in the fishing boats. Nor can he call his Helen “the face that launched a thousand dinghies.” Lacks grandeur, that phrase. What he can do, though, is place them in situations where their nobility and their courage are put to the test, while reminding us that they are acting out some of the most basic, most primal patterns known to humans, exactly as Homer did all those centuries before. The need to protect one’s family: Hector. The need to maintain one’s dignity: Achilles. The determination to remain faithful and to have faith: Penelope. The struggle to return home: Odysseus. Homer gives us four great struggles of the human being: with nature, with the divine, with other humans, and with ourselves. What is there, after all, against which we need to prove ourselves but those four things? 
In our modern world, of course, parallels may be ironized, that is, turned on their head for
purposes of irony. How many of us would see the comedy of three escaped convicts as parallel to the wanderings of Odysseus? Still, that’s what brothers Joel and Ethan Coen give us in their 2000 film O Brother, Where Art Thou? It’s about trying to get home, isn’t it? Or this, the most famous example: a single day in Dublin in 1904, on which a young man decides on his future and an older man wanders the city, eventually returning home to his wife in the small hours of the next morning. The book has only one overt clue that this all might have something to do with Homer, its one-word title: Ulysses (1922). As we now know, James Joyce envisioned every one of the eighteen episodes of the novel as a parallel to some incident or situation in The Odyssey. There’s an episode in a newspaper office, for instance, which parallels Odysseus’s visit to Aeolus, the god of the winds, but the parallel may seem pretty tenuous. To be sure, newspapermen are a windy group and there are a lot of rhetorical flourishes in the episode, to say nothing of the fact that a gust of wind does zip through at one point. Still, we can see it as resembling the Homeric original only if we understand that resemblance in terms of a funhouse mirror, full of distortion and goofy correspondences—if we understand it, in other words, as an ironic parallel. The fact that it’s ironic makes the parallel—and the Aeolus episode—such fun. Joyce is less interested than Walcott in investing his characters with classical nobility, although finally they do take on something of that quality. After watching poor old Leopold Bloom stroll around Dublin all day and half the night, running into no end of trouble and recalling great heartbreak in his life, we may well come to feel he is noble in his own way. His nobility, however, is not that of Odysseus. 
Greek and Roman myth, of course, is more than Homer. The transformations of Ovid’s Metamorphoses show up in all sorts of later works, not least in Franz Kafka’s story of a man who wakes up one morning to find he’s changed into an enormous beetle. He called it “The Metamorphosis.” Indiana Jones may look like pure Hollywood, but the intrepid searcher after fabulous treasure goes back to Apollonius and The Argonautica, the story of Jason and the Argonauts. Something a bit homier? Sophocles’ plays of Oedipus and his doomed clan show up over and over again in all sorts of variations. There is, in fact, no form of dysfunctional family or no personal disintegration of character for which there is not a Greek or Roman model. Not for nothing do the names of Greek tragic characters figure in Freud’s theories. The wronged woman gone violent in her grief and madness? Would you like Aeneas and Dido or Jason and Medea? And as in every good early religion, they had an explanation for natural phenomena, from the change of seasons (Demeter and Persephone and Hades) to why the nightingale sounds the way it does (Philomena and Tereus). Happily for us, most of it got written down, often in several versions, so that we have access to this wonderful body of story. And because writers and readers share knowledge of a big portion of this body of story, this mythology, when writers use it, we readers recognize it, sometimes to its full extent, sometimes only dimly or only because we know the Looney Tunes version. That recognition makes our experience of literature richer, deeper, more meaningful, so that our own modern stories also matter, also share in the power of myth. 
Among the more interesting recent developments in writing for younger readers is the Percy Jackson and the Olympians series by Rick Riordan. The quintet of novels begins with The Lightning Thief (2005). Percy is a misfit kid who finds out he’s the son of Poseidon and is accused of stealing
Zeus’s weapon of choice, the lightning bolt. Then he finds out his pal is a satyr, fights a minotaur, and befriends a daughter of Athena, and all Hades breaks loose. As a demigod, Percy has issues with normality (things like ADHD and dyslexia), but he’s the real deal on the hero front, as he gets a chance to prove over and over. His divine bloodlines help, as do his mythic buddies. It’s one thing, you know, to be the offspring of a former star pupil at your wizarding prep school, but to have the sea god as your dad, well . . . 
Oh, did I forget to say? That title of Walcott’s, Omeros? In the local dialect, it means Homer. Naturally.

البته در فرهنگ‌های اروپایی و اروپایی-آمریکایی، منبع دیگری برای اسطوره وجود دارد. بگذارید دوباره بگویم: **اسطوره**. وقتی بیشتر ما به «اسطوره» می‌اندیشیم، منظورمان کرانه‌های شمالی مدیترانه در دو تا سه هزار سال پیش است. منظورمان یونان و روم است. اسطوره‌های یونانی و رومی چنان در تاروپود آگاهی – و در واقع ناخودآگاه – ما تنیده شده‌اند که به ندرت متوجه‌شان می‌شویم. شک دارید؟ در شهری که من زندگی می‌کنم، تیم‌های دانشگاهی با نام «اسپارتان‌ها» شناخته می‌شوند. دبیرستان ما؟ «تروجان‌ها». در ایالت ما شهرهایی به نام تروی (که یکی از دبیرستان‌هایش آتن است – و می‌گویند در آموزش‌وپرورش کمدین وجود ندارد)، ایتاکا، اسپارتا، رومولوس، رموس و رم وجود دارد. این جوامع در سراسر ایالت پراکنده‌اند و به دوره‌های مختلف اسکان بازمی‌گردند. حال اگر شهری در مرکز میشیگان، در فاصله‌ای قابل توجه از هر چیزی که بتوان اژه‌ای یا یونانی نامید (هرچند از شهر آیونیا چندان دور نیست)، بتواند ایتاکا نامیده شود، نشان می‌دهد که اسطوره یونانی قدرت ماندگاری بسیار خوبی داشته است.  

بگذارید لحظه‌ای به تونی موریسون بازگردم. من همیشه کمی شگفت‌زده می‌شوم که ایکاروس تمام توجه را به خود جلب می‌کند. این پدرش، ددالوس بود که بال‌ها را ساخت، که می‌دانست چگونه از کرت بگریزد و به سلامت به سرزمین اصلی برسد، و در واقع به سلامت پرواز کرد. ایکاروس، آن نوجوان ماجراجو، نتوانست از توصیه پدرش پیروی کند و سقوط کرد و جان باخت. سقوط او منبع جذابیت پایدار برای ما و برای ادبیات و هنرمان باقی مانده است. در آن چیزهای بسیاری می‌بینیم: تلاش والدین برای نجات فرزند و اندوه ناشی از ناکامی، درمانی که به مرگبار بودنِ بیماری ثابت می‌شود، شور و نشاط جوانی که به خودویرانی می‌انجامد، تقابل خرد خردمندانه بزرگسالان و بی‌پروایی نوجوانان، و البته هراسِ ناشی از آن سقوط سرنگون‌شونده به دریا. هیچ‌کدام از این‌ها ربطی به موریسون و آفریقایی‌های پرنده‌اش ندارد، پس جای شگفتی نیست که او از این واکنش خوانندگانش کمی سردرگم می‌شود. اما این داستان و الگو چنان در آگاهی ما رخنه کرده که خوانندگان تقریباً به‌طور خودکار هر زمان که پرواز یا سقوط برانگیخته می‌شود، آن را به یاد می‌آورند. آشکارا با موقعیت در «سرود سلیمان» همخوانی ندارد. اما در آثار دیگر مصداق دارد. در سال ۱۵۵۸، پیتر بروگل نقاشی شگفت‌انگیزی کشید به نام «چشمانداز با سقوط ایکاروس». در پیش‌زمینه دهقانی و گاوش را می‌بینیم، کمی آن‌سوتر چوپانی و گله‌اش، و در دریا کشتی بازرگانی که به آرامی در حرکت است؛ این صحنه‌ای است از معمولیت و آرامش مطلق. تنها در گوشه پایین سمت راست نقاشی است که چیزی حتی از دور هم حاکی از مشکل دیده می‌شود: جفت پاهایی کج‌و‌معوج که در حال ناپدید شدن در آب هستند. این پسر ماست. او واقعاً حضوری چشمگیر در قاب ندارد، اما حضورش همه‌چیز را دگرگون می‌کند. بدون حزن‌انگیزی پسر محکوم‌به‌مرگ، تصویری داریم از کشاورزی و کشتیرانی بازرگانی بدون هیچ قدرت روایی یا درون‌مایه‌ای. من به‌طور منظم دو شعر بزرگ را که بر اساس آن نقاشی سروده شده‌اند تدریس می‌کنم: «موزه هنرهای زیبا» (۱۹۴۰) اثر دبلیو. اچ. اودن و «چشمانداز با سقوط ایکاروس» (۱۹۶۲) اثر ویلیام کارلوس ویلیامز. آنها اشعار شگفت‌انگیزی هستند، با لحن، سبک و فرمی بسیار متفاوت از یکدیگر، اما در توافق اساسی درباره اینکه جهان چگونه حتی در مواجهه با تراژدی‌های خصوصی ما به راه خود ادامه می‌دهد. هر هنرمند آنچه را در نقاشی یافته تغییر می‌دهد. بروگل دهقان و کشتی را وارد می‌کند، که هیچ‌کدام در روایتی که از یونانیان به ما رسیده ظاهر نمی‌شوند. و ویلیامز و اودن به نوبه خود، عناصر کمی متفاوتی را در نقاشی برای تأکید می‌یابند. شعر ویلیامز بر عناصر تصویری نقاشی تأکید می‌کند و می‌کوشد صحنه را ثبت کند در حالی که عناصر درون‌مایه‌ای را پنهانی وارد می‌کند. حتی چینش شعرش در صفحه، باریک و بسیار عمودی، بدن در حال سقوط از آسمان را به یاد می‌آورد. از سوی دیگر، شعر اودن تأملی است بر ماهیت خصوصی رنج و نحوه‌ای که جهان بزرگتر هیچ علاقه‌ای به فجایع خصوصی ما نشان نمی‌دهد. شگفت‌انگیز و خوشایند است که کشف کنیم نقاشی می‌تواند موجب این دو واکنش بسیار متفاوت شود. فراتر از آنها، خوانندگان پیام‌های خود را در این میان می‌یابند. به عنوان کسی که در دهه شصت نوجوان بود، سرنوشت ایکاروس مرا به یاد همه آن نوجوانانی می‌اندازد که خودروهای عضلانی با نام‌هایی مانند موستانگ، فایربرد، چارجر و باراکودا خریدند. همه آموزش‌های رانندگی و توصیه‌های استوار والدین در جهان نمی‌توانند بر جذابیت آن‌گونه قدرت غلبه کنند، و متأسفانه، در موارد بسیار زیادی آن رانندگان جوان سرنوشت ایکاروس را تجربه کردند. دانش‌آموزانم، که کمی از من جوان‌ترند، ناگزیر مشابهت‌های دیگری خواهند یافت. با این حال، همه این‌ها به اسطوره بازمی‌گردد: پسر، بال‌ها، شیرجه ناخواسته.  

پس این یکی از راه‌هایی است که اسطوره کلاسیک می‌تواند عمل کند: موضوع عینی اشعار، نقاشی‌ها، اپراها و رمان‌ها. اسطوره چه کار دیگری می‌تواند بکند؟  

اینجا فکری هست. فرض کنید می‌خواستید شعری حماسی درباره جامعه‌ای از ماهیگیران فقیر در کارائیب بنویسید. اگر این جایی بود که از آن آمده بودید و این مردم را مثل خانواده خود می‌شناختید، می‌خواستید حسادت‌ها، کینه‌ها، ماجراجویی و خطر را به تصویر بکشید، و همچنین شأن و زندگیشان را به گونه‌ای ثبت کنید که همه آنچه از دید گردشگران و صاحبان ملک سفیدپوست پنهان مانده را منتقل کند. می‌توانستید، گمان می‌کنم، سعی کنید بسیار بسیار جدی باشید، شخصیت‌ها را بسیار جدی و متین به تصویر بکشید، و با فضیلت نیک‌خواهی‌شان آنها را نجیب جلوه دهید. اما شرط می‌بندم که جواب نمی‌داد. آنچه در نهایت به دست می‌آوردید احتمالاً بسیار خشک و تصنعی می‌شد، و تصنع هرگز نجیب نیست. گذشته از این، این مردم قدیس نیستند. آنها اشتباهات زیادی مرتکب می‌شوند: خرده‌بین، حسود، شهوت‌پرست، گاه طمعکار و همچنین شجاع، ظریف، قدرتمند، آگاه و ژرف‌نگر هستند. و شما در نهایت نجابت می‌خواهید، نه تونتو – هیچ رنجر تنهایی اینجا نیست. به‌آن‌ترتیب، ممکن است سعی کنید داستانشان را بر روی داستان کهن‌تری از رقابت و خشونت پیوند بزنید، داستانی که حتی پیروز در نهایت محکوم به نابودی است، داستانی که در آن، علیرغم کاستی‌های گاه شخصی، شخصیت‌ها نجابتی بی‌چون‌و‌چرا دارند. می‌توانید به شخصیت‌هایتان نام‌هایی مانند هلن، فیلوکتتس، هکتور و آشیل بدهید. حداقل این کاری است که برنده نوبل، دریک والکات، در «اومروس» (۱۹۹۰) خود انجام می‌دهد. این نام‌ها، البته، از ایلیاد گرفته شده‌اند، هرچند والکات از عناصر – هم‌نشینی‌ها، اشخاص و موقعیت‌های – هر دو آن و ادیسه در حماسه خود استفاده می‌کند.  

سؤالی که ناگزیر خواهیم پرسید این است: چرا؟  

چرا کسی در اواخر سده بیستم باید به داستانی رجوع کند که به صورت شفاهی از سده دوازدهم تا هشتم پیش از میلاد منتقل شده و شاید تا دویست یا سیصد سال بعد مکتوب نشده است؟ چرا کسی باید سعی کند ماهیگیران مدرن را با این قهرمانان افسانه‌ای مقایسه کند، که بسیاری از آنها از نسل خدایان بودند؟ خوب، برای شروع، قهرمانان افسانه‌ای هومر کشاورز و ماهیگیر بودند. گذشته از این، مگر نه اینکه همه ما از نسل خدایانیم؟ والکات با این هم‌نشینی به ما یادآوری می‌کند که پتانسیل عظمت در همه ما وجود دارد، صرف‌نظر از اینکه شرایط دنیوی‌ چقدر فروتنانه باشد.  

این یک پاسخ است. پاسخ دیگر این است که موقعیت‌ها بیش از آنچه انتظار داریم با هم مطابقت دارند. طرح ایلیاد چندان الهی یا جهانی نیست. کسانی که هرگز آن را نخوانده‌اند به اشتباه گمان می‌برند که داستان جنگ تروا است. نیست. داستان یک کنش واحد و نسبتاً طولانی است: خشم آشیل (فقط پنجاه‌و‌سه روز از ده سال). آشیل بر رهبرش، آگاممنون، خشم می‌گیرد، پشتیبانی خود را از یونانیان پس می‌گیرد، و تنها زمانی به نبرد بازمی‌گردد که پیامدهای عملش بهترین دوستش، پاتروکلوس، را نابود کرده است. در این نقطه خشم خود را متوجه تروایی‌ها و به‌ویژه بزرگترین قهرمانشان، هکتور، می‌کند که در نهایت او را می‌کشد. دلیل چنین خشم‌اش؟ آگاممنون غنیمت جنگی‌اش را گرفته است. پیش‌پاافتاده؟ بدتر می‌شود. غنیمت یک زن است. آگاممنون، که به دستور الهی و احساسات عمومی مجبور به بازگرداندن معشوقه‌اش به پدرش می‌شود، علیه کسی که آشکارترین مخالفت را با او کرده بود، آشیل، با گرفتن معشوقه‌اش، بریسئیس، تلافی می‌کند. به اندازه کافی خرده‌بینانه است؟ نجیبانه است؟ هیچ هلنی، هیچ داوری پاریس، هیچ اسب تروا. در هسته خود، داستان مردی است که به خاطر مصادره عروس جنگی دزدیده‌شده‌اش خشمگین می‌شود، که در پس‌ای از کشتار گسترده اجرا می‌شود، که کل آن به این دلیل رخ می‌دهد که مرد دیگری، منلائوس (برادر آگاممنون)، همسرش توسط پاریس، برادر ناتنی هکتور، دزدیده شده است. اینگونه است که هکتور ناگزیر می‌شود امیدهای نجات کل تروا را بر دوش بکشد.  

و با این حال به نحوی، در طول سده‌ها، این داستان که با دزدی دو زن تسخیر شده، به تجسم ایده‌آل‌های قهرمانی و وفاداری، فداکاری و ازدست‌دادن بدل شده است. هکتور در کار محکوم‌به‌شکستش سرسختانه‌تر از هر کسی که دیده‌اید قهرمان است. اندوه آشیل بر ازدست‌دادن دوست محبوبش واقعاً دل‌اشک‌بار است. دوئل‌های بزرگ – بین هکتور و آژاکس، بین دیومدس و پاریس، بین هکتور و پاتروکلوس، بین هکتور و آشیل – به‌راستی هیجان‌انگیز و پرتعلیق هستند، و پیامدهایشان منبعی از جشن‌و‌شادی و ناامیدی بزرگ. جای شگفتی نیست که بسیاری از نویسندگان مدرن اغلب از هومر وام گرفته‌اند و از او تقلید کرده‌اند.  

و این چه زمانی آغاز شد؟  

تقریباً بلافاصله. ویرژیل، که در ۱۹ پیش از میلاد درگذشت، آینیاس خود را بر اساس قهرمانان هومری الگوبرداری کرد. اگر آشیل کاری کرد یا اودیسه جایی رفت، آینیاس هم می‌کند. چرا؟ این کاری است که قهرمانان می‌کنند. آینیاس به جهان اموات می‌رود. چرا؟ اودیسه رفت. او در نبرد اوج نهایی غولی از اردوگاه دشمن را می‌کشد. چرا؟ آشیل این کار را کرد. و الی آخر. کل ماجرا کمتر از آنچه به نظر می‌رسد اقتباسی است و خالی از طنز و کنایه نیست. آینیاس و پیروانش بازماندگان تروا هستند، پس در اینجا این قهرمان تروایی داریم که الگوهای تعیین‌شده توسط دشمنانش را اجرا می‌کند. افزون بر این، وقتی این تروایی‌ها از کنار ایتاکا، خانه اودیسه، می‌گذرند، به عامل نابودی‌شان ناسزا می‌گویند و لعن‌ش می‌کنند. اما به‌طور کلی، ویرژیل او را به این کنش‌ها وامیدارد زیرا هومر پیش‌تر تعریف کرده بود که قهرمان بودن چه معنایی دارد.  

بازگردیم به والکات. تقریباً دقیقاً دو هزار سال پس از ویرژیل، والکات قهرمانانش را به انجام کنش‌هایی واداشته که می‌توانیم به عنوان بازاجرایی نمادین کنش‌های هومر تشخیص دهیم. گاه کمی کشش دارد، چون نمی‌توانیم دوئل‌های زیادی در میدان نبرد در قایق‌های ماهیگیری داشته باشیم. و نه می‌تواند هلنش را «چهره‌ای که هزار قایق پارویی را به آب انداخت» بنامد. آن عبارت شکوه ندارد. اما آنچه می‌تواند بکند، قرار دادن آنها در موقعیت‌هایی است که نجابت و شجاعت‌ محک می‌خورد، در حالی که به ما یادآوری می‌کند که آنها برخی از بنیادی‌ترین و اصیل‌ترین الگوهای شناخته‌شده برای انسان را اجرا می‌کنند، دقیقاً همانطور که هومر قرن‌ها پیش انجام داد. نیاز به محافظت از خانواده: هکتور. نیاز به حفظ شأن: آشیل. عزم به وفادار ماندن و وفاداری داشتن: پنلوپه. تلاش برای بازگشت به خانه: اودیسه. هومر چهار مبارزه بزرگ انسان را به ما می‌دهد: با طبیعت، با امر الوهی، با دیگر انسان‌ها و با خودمان. در نهایت، چه چیزی وجود دارد که نیاز داشته باشیم خود را در برابر آن ثابت کنیم جز این چهار چیز؟  

البته در جهان مدرن ما، هم‌نشینی‌ها ممکن است آیرونایز (ironized) شوند، یعنی برای مقاصد کنایه‌ای وارونه شوند. چند نفر از ما کمدی سه زند فراری را موازی با سرگردانی‌های اودیسه می‌بینیم؟ با این حال، این همان چیزی است که برادران جوئل و ایتان کوئن در فیلم ۲۰۰۰ خود «ای برادر، کجایی؟» به ما ارائه می‌دهند. این درباره تلاش برای رسیدن به خانه است، نیست؟ یا این، مشهورترین مثال: یک روز واحد در دوبلین در سال ۱۹۰۴، که در آن مردی جوان درباره آینده‌اش تصمیم می‌گیرد و مردی مسن‌تر در شهر سرگردان است، و در نهایت سحرگاه روز بعد به خانه نزد همسرش بازمی‌گردد. کتاب تنها یک سرنخ آشکار دارد که همه اینها ممکن است ربطی به هومر داشته باشد، عنوان تک‌واژه‌اش: اولیس (۱۹۲۲). همانطور که اکنون می‌دانیم، جیمز جویس هر یک از هجده اپیزود رمان را موازی با حادثه‌ای یا موقعیتی در ادیسه تصور کرد. برای مثال، اپیزودی در دفتر روزنامه وجود دارد که موازی با دیدار اودیسه از آیولوس، خدای بادهاست، اما این هم‌نشینی ممکن است بسیار سست به نظر برسد. مسلماً، روزنامه‌نگاران گروهی پرگو هستند و در این اپیزود جلوه‌های بلاغی زیادی وجود دارد، گذشته از این واقعیت که نسیمی در یک نقطه با سرعت می‌وزد. با این حال، تنها در صورتی می‌توانیم آن را شبیه به اصل هومری ببینیم که این شباهت را در آینه‌های کج‌و‌معوج خانه‌های سرگرمی بفهمیم، پر از تحریف و هم‌نشینی‌های مسخره – به عبارت دیگر، اگر آن را به عنوان هم‌نشینی کنایه‌ای بفهمیم. این واقعیت که کنایه‌ای است، هم‌نشینی – و اپیزود آیولوس – را چنین لذت‌بخش می‌کند. جویس کمتر از والکات علاقه‌مند است که به شخصیت‌�هایش نجابت کلاسیک ببخشد، هرچند در نهایت آنها چیزی از آن کیفیت را به خود می‌گیرند. پس از تماشای لئوپولد بلومِ بی‌چاره که تمام روز و نیمی از شب در دوبلین پرسه می‌زند، با بی‌پایان دردسر مواجه می‌شود و اندوه‌های بزرگ زندگی‌اش را به یاد می‌آورد، به خوبی ممکن است احساس کنیم که او به شیوه خود نجیب است. اما نجابت او، نجابت اودیسه نیست.  

اسطوره یونانی و رومی، البته، فراتر از هومر است. دگردیسی‌های «دگردیسی‌ها» اثر اووید در انواع آثار بعدی ظاهر می‌شوند، به‌ویژه در داستان فرانتس کافکا درباره مردی که یک صبح بیدار می‌شود و می‌بیند به سوسک غول‌پیکری تبدیل شده است. او آن را «مسخ» نامید. ایندیانا جونز ممکن است کاملاً هالیوودی به نظر برسد، اما جستجوگر بی‌باک گنج‌های افسانه‌ای به آپولونیوس و «آرگوناتیکا»، داستان جیسون و آرگونات‌ها، بازمی‌گردد. چیزی کمی خودمانی‌تر؟ نمایش‌های سوفوکل درباره ادیپ و خاندان محکوم‌به‌نابودی‌اش بارها و بارها در انواع واریاسیون‌ها ظاهر می‌شوند. در واقع، هیچ شکلی از خانواده ناکارآمد یا هیچ فروپاشی شخصیتی فردی وجود ندارد که مدل یونانی یا رومی برای آن وجود نداشته باشد. بی‌جهت نیست که نام شخصیت‌های تراژیک یونانی در نظریه‌های فروید ظاهر می‌شوند. زن بی‌عدالتی‌دیده که در اندوه و جنونش خشن شده است؟ آیا آینیاس و دیدو را می‌خواهید یا جیسون و مدیا؟ و مانند هر دین اولیه خوبی، توضیحی برای پدیده‌های طبیعی داشتند، از تغییر فصل‌ها (دمتر و پرسفونه و هادس) تا اینکه چرا بلبل صدایش آنگونه است (فیلومنا و تریوس). خوشبختانه برای ما، بیشتر آن مکتوب شد، اغلب در چندین نسخه، تا به این ساختار روایی شگفت‌انگیز دسترسی داشته باشیم. و چون نویسندگان و خوانندگان دانش بخش بزرگی از این ساختار روایی، این اسطوره‌شناسی، را به اشتراک می‌گذارند، وقتی نویسندگان از آن استفاده می‌کنند، ما خوانندگان آن را تشخیص می‌دهیم، گاه به طور کامل، گاه فقط مبهم یا فقط به این دلیل که نسخه لونی تونز (Looney Tunes) را می‌شناسیم. این تشخیص تجربه ما از ادبیات را غنی‌تر، عمیق‌تر، معنادارتر می‌سازد، به‌طوری که داستان‌های مدرن خودمان نیز اهمیت می‌یابند و در قدرت اسطوره شریک می‌شوند.  

از میان جالب‌ترین تحولات اخیر در نوشتن برای خوانندگان جوان، مجموعه «پرسی جکسون و المپنشین‌ها» اثر ریک ریوردن است. پنج‌گانه رمان‌ها با «دزد صاعقه» (۲۰۰۵) آغاز می‌شود. پرسی نوجوانی است که نمی‌تواند جایی برای خود پیدا کند و می‌فهمد پسر پوزیدون است و متهم به دزدیدن سلاح برگزیده زئوس، صاعقه، شده است. سپس می‌فهمد دوستش ساتیر است، با مینوتور می‌جنگد، با دختری از آتنا دوست می‌شود، و همه جهنم به پا می‌شود. به عنوان یک نیمه‌خدا، پرسی با عادی‌بودن مشکل دارد (چیزهایی مانند ADHD و دیسلکسیا)، اما در جبهه قهرمانی واقعی است، همانطور که بارها و بارها فرصت اثباتش را می‌یابد. تبار الهی‌اش کمک می‌کند، همانطور که دوستان اسطوره‌ای‌اش. یک چیز است، می‌دانید، فرزند شاگرد ستاره‌دار سابق در مدرسه آمادگی جادوگری‌تان باشید، اما خدای دریا را پدر داشته باشید، خب...  

آه، فراموش کردم بگویم؟ آن عنوان والکات، «اومروس»؟ در گویش محلی، به معنای هومر است. طبیعتاً.

**The Lingering Shadow of the Sorrow King: Holden Caulfield’s Enduring Influence on Literary Disillusionment**  

J.D. Salinger’s *The Catcher in the Rye* (1951) irrevocably altered the literary landscape, introducing Holden Caulfield—a prototypical figure of adolescent disenchantment—whose raw emotionality, caustic worldview, and confessional narrative voice became a blueprint for subsequent authors. In the decades following the novel’s publication, writers have endeavored to replicate Holden’s essence, crafting protagonists who mirror his existential angst, confrontations with mortality, and fractured idealism. This emulation has spawned a subgenre of literature dominated by what might be termed “sorrow kings”: characters steeped in melancholic introspection, whose narratives dissect societal hypocrisy and personal trauma. Through works such as Stephen Chbosky’s *The Perks of Being a Wallflower* (1999) and Sylvia Plath’s *The Bell Jar* (1963), authors have channeled Holden’s legacy, weaving his thematic and stylistic DNA into their protagonists’ psyches, albeit with varying degrees of originality and depth.  

Chbosky’s Charlie, the introspective epistolary narrator of *The Perks of Being a Wallflower*, epitomizes this homage. Like Holden, Charlie is a social outsider whose laconic cynicism masks profound vulnerability. His letters—fraught with references to suicide, sexual awakening, and psychological trauma—echo Holden’s disjointed monologues, blending wry observation with visceral despair. Charlie’s fixation on his deceased friend Michael, whose suicide haunts the narrative, mirrors Holden’s obsession with his brother Allie’s death, underscoring a shared preoccupation with mortality as both a metaphysical quandary and a personal specter. Furthermore, Charlie’s navigation of adolescent sexuality—marked by awkward encounters and latent trauma—parallels Holden’s ambivalence toward intimacy, reflecting a broader critique of societal expectations. Chbosky’s deliberate invocation of Salinger’s voice, however, transcends mere imitation; it recontextualizes Holden’s disillusionment within the grunge-era 1990s, illustrating how existential disquiet persists across generations.  

Similarly, Sylvia Plath’s Esther Greenwood in *The Bell Jar* channels Holden’s caustic introspection, albeit through a distinctly gendered lens. Esther’s descent into mental illness—punctuated by suicide attempts, electroshock therapy, and a suffocating sense of societal entrapment—mirrors Holden’s psychological unraveling. Her scathing critiques of 1950s conformity (“I saw the years of my life spaced along a road in the form of telephone poles, threaded together by wires”) recall Holden’s diatribes against “phonies,” yet Plath amplifies the stakes by embedding Esther’s struggles within patriarchal constraints. Where Holden’s angst stems from a loss of innocence, Esther’s arises from the collision between intellectual ambition and rigid gender roles—a nuance that expands Salinger’s template. The Bell Jar’s clinical prose, interspersed with surreal imagery, diverges from Holden’s colloquial digressions, yet both narratives converge in their unflinching portrayal of protagonists teetering on the precipice of self-annihilation.  

The proliferation of such characters—including the unnamed narrator of *Catcher Caught* (a lesser-known but thematically resonant work)—reveals both the potency and limitations of Salinger’s influence. While these narratives adeptly replicate Holden’s voice and motifs, they risk eclipsing innovation with derivativeness. INT. OLD LADY INTERIOR - DAY

The interior of the Old Lady is an eclectic mix of Edwardian charm and alien technology, all brass fittings, and pulsating alien lights. At the controls stands JOYCE GRENFELL, the 1st Traveller, with a look of weary exasperation that belies her years, her hair tucked up in a sensible bun, and her apparel a cross between a governess and an explorer.

Three students — VIVIAN, a bright-eyed young woman played by Carol Ann Ford, and her two friends, a curious girl with an assertive gaze, and a lanky boy with a mop of hair and a questioning look — stand awkwardly nearby. They're clearly out of their element, both fascinated and nervous about the interior of this impossible machine.

TRAVELLER (Joyce Grenfell)
(eyeing the newcomers disapprovingly)
Well, I suppose introductions are in order since you've made yourselves quite at home in my sanctuary. You may call me the Traveller.

The Old Lady starts to whirr and vibrate, the sound is otherworldly, and the lights shift in color and intensity.

VIVIAN
Miss Traveller, you have to understand, we were just concerned—

TRAVELLER (interrupting sternly)
Concerned? And what, pray tell, necessitates barging into a person's vestibule uninvited?

FEMALE STUDENT FRIEND
(stepping forward, trying to sound confident)
We saw Vivian walk in, and... and it vanished right in front of our eyes! We had to see if she was alright.

MALE STUDENT FRIEND
(mutters to the female friend)
Not our brightest move.

TRAVELLER
Vanished, you say? Oh, heavens.

The boy looks around, still in disbelief of his surroundings, trying to grasp what his eyes are seeing.

MALE STUDENT FRIEND
This is... there’s no way... it’s bigger on the inside!

TRAVELLER (sighing)
Yes, yes. A spatial anomaly — but that's beside the point. You are? Names, please.

VIVIAN
This is Anne and that's John. Miss Traveller, they're my friends from uni. They wouldn't have come if they didn't care.

TRAVELLER (softening ever so slightly)
Vivian, my dear, I am not an ogre. It's just... The Old Lady isn't accustomed to... unexpected guests. She can be quite temperamental.

Suddenly, there's a loud clunk, and the Old Lady lurches, causing everyone to stagger. Anne clings to a railing, John catches his balance against a wall, and Vivian steps closer to the Traveller, looking for an explanation.

TRAVELLER (with a brisk tone)
Well, since we’re all here, it would be rude to not offer a trip. But make no mistake; this is not a joyride.

VIVIAN
(excitedly, to her friends)
You're going to see! It's incredible!

TRAVELLER (addressing all three)
If you're to come along, know this — curiosity is a fine thing, but it comes with a responsibility. There will be rules to follow, and it won't all be fun and games.

The Old Lady steadies and a soft hum replaces the violent shaking. The Traveller turns her attention to the controls, fiddling with dials with a practiced hand.

TRAVELLER (continuing, more to herself)
Now, where to first? Ah, yes. The perfect place for wide-eyed novices...

A beat, as the Traveller fixes her gaze on her unexpected companions, each of them now brimming with a mix of anticipation and trepidation.

TRAVELLER (smirking)
Welcome aboard the Old Lady, my unlikely crew.

With a final lever pulled, the machine lurches once more. A symphony of alien sounds envelope the room as they launch into the vortex, the adventure beginning anew.

The intertwining of Joyce Grenfell's wry, motherly warmth and authoritative spirit sets the tone for what promises to be a journey unlike any these students have ever imagined. The Traveller, an enigmatic figure leading them into the unknown, watches over her new companions as the Old Lady travels onwards through time and space.

FADE OUT.

**XI. Ongoing Digital Minimalism Practices**  
*(Minimalist Tone: Clear, Purposeful, Uncluttered)*  

Digital minimalism is not a one-time purge but a sustained commitment to aligning technology with your values. Below are actionable practices to maintain clarity-first habits in a hyperconnected world, with examples to illustrate their real-world application.  

---

### **1. Regular Digital Audits**  
**Principle:** Periodically reassess your tools and habits to eliminate drift into mindless consumption.  
- **Action:** Conduct a 10-minute audit every 3 months. Ask:  
  - *Which apps/websites added value in the last 90 days?*  
  - *What distracted me most?*  
- **Example:**  
  - Delete social media apps used solely for passive scrolling (e.g., Instagram), but keep messaging tools that nurture close relationships (e.g., WhatsApp for family chats).  
  - Turn off non-essential notifications (e.g., news alerts) while retaining calendar reminders.  

---

### **2. Intentional Onboarding**  
**Principle:** Treat new technology like a guest—invite only what serves a clear purpose.  
- **Action:** Use a **24-hour rule** before downloading apps or subscribing to services. Ask:  
  - *Does this solve a specific problem?*  
  - *Will it replace or duplicate an existing tool?*  
- **Example:**  
  - Instead of impulsively buying a meditation app, test free alternatives (e.g., Insight Timer) for a week before committing.  
  - Decline "convenience" apps (e.g., a coffee-ordering app) if you visit the café once a month.  

---

### **3. Friction-Based Design**  
**Principle:** Make distraction inconvenient; prioritize effortful access to low-value tools.  
- **Action:**  
  - Move non-essential apps to a secondary screen or folder titled “Think Twice.”  
  - Enable grayscale mode on your phone to reduce visual allure.  
- **Example:**  
  - Keep TikTok in a hidden folder, requiring 3 swipes to access. By the time you reach it, the urge to scroll often passes.  
  - Use a password manager with a long master password to deter casual logins to entertainment sites.  

---

### **4. Scheduled Connectivity**  
**Principle:** Batch digital tasks into focused blocks to reclaim uninterrupted time.  
- **Action:** Designate 2–3 daily windows for emails/social media (e.g., 9 AM, 1 PM, 5 PM). Outside these, close tabs and silence devices.  
- **Example:**  
  - A writer checks Slack only after completing a 3-hour morning writing session.  
  - A parent disables work email after 7 PM to prioritize family dinners.  

---

### **5. Analog Alternatives**  
**Principle:** Replace digital habits with tactile, screen-free rituals.  
- **Action:** Identify one digital dependency to swap weekly (e.g., e-books → physical books, Spotify → vinyl records).  
- **Example:**  
  - Instead of a Netflix binge, host a board game night with friends.  
  - Replace morning news scrolling with a printed newspaper and coffee.  

---

### **6. Mindful Consumption**  
**Principle:** Curate inputs to protect attention and mental space.  
- **Action:**  
  - Unfollow accounts that trigger comparison or dissatisfaction.  
  - Use RSS feeds or newsletters (not algorithms) to control information intake.  
- **Example:**  
  - Prune Instagram follows from 500 to 30 accounts that inspire creativity (e.g., artists, mentors).  
  - Replace YouTube’s with a curated playlist of educational podcasts.  

---

### **7. Tech-Free Zones**

Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) on hemodialysis present unique challenges when managing conditions such as Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) due to altered pharmacokinetics, increased risk of drug accumulation, and potential interactions with their existing treatment regimen. When treating IBS in this patient population, both the efficacy of the medication and its safety profile in CKD must be considered.

### General Considerations

- **Assessment**: Before prescribing, a thorough assessment is necessary to rule out other causes of his symptoms that might mimic IBS, such as electrolyte imbalances or medications that could contribute to his symptoms.
- **Non-pharmacological Management**: Initially, managing IBS in patients on hemodialysis should focus on non-pharmacological approaches, including dietary modifications (low FODMAP diet), ensuring adequate fiber intake (taking into account potential restrictions due to hemodialysis), hydration as allowed for his fluid restriction, and regular exercise as tolerated.

### Medication Options

Given your patient's condition (hemodialysis-dependency), drug removal by dialysis, altered drug metabolism, and potential drug accumulation must be considered.

#### For Constipation-Predominant Symptoms:

- **Psyllium**: A soluble fiber that can help both constipation and diarrhea but needs to be introduced gradually and with adequate water intake within his fluid restriction limits. Monitor potassium as some fiber supplements might contain significant amounts.
- **Pegylated Laxative (Polyethylene Glycol, PEG)**: Generally considered safe in patients on hemodialysis and does not significantly accumulate in CKD.

#### For Diarrhea-Predominant Symptoms:

- **Loperamide**: Can be used carefully for diarrhea control, but start at a low dose and adjust based on symptom control and tolerance. Monitor for potential side effects, like abdominal distension or constipation.
- **Rifaximin**: Although primarily used for hepatic encephalopathy and traveler's diarrhea, it has shown efficacy in IBS-D as well. The renal adjustment is not typically required, but use with caution and monitor for efficacy and adverse effects.

### Medications to Use With Caution or Avoid

- **Antispasmodics** (e.g., dicyclomine, hyoscyamine): These can be used but with caution due to potential anticholinergic side effects.
- **TCA Antidepressants** (e.g., amitriptyline): Can be used in very low doses for their analgesic properties in IBS but need careful monitoring for side effects, given their anticholinergic properties and potential for accumulation in CKD.
- **5-HT3 antagonists** (e.g., Alosetron): Specific use in severe IBS-D but requires careful consideration due to potential side effects and the need for monitoring.

### Monitoring and Adjustment

It’s crucial to closely monitor the patient for any side effects, efficacy of the treatment, and potential interactions with his other medications. Adjustments may be necessary based on his response and any changes in his hemodialysis regimen.

### Collaboration

Given the complexity of managing a hemodialysis patient with IBS, collaboration with a multidisciplinary team including nephrologists, dietitians, and possibly a gastroenterologist is advised to ensure optimal care.

### Final Note

For specific medication dosages and further individualized treatment plans, always refer to updated clinical guidelines and consider consulting with specialists when necessary. The pharmacokinetic profile of each drug can significantly differ in patients with CKD and on dialysis, thus close monitoring for efficacy and toxicity is paramount.

Given the complexity of your patient's health status, the information provided here serves as a general guide and must be adapted to the individual patient's needs and health status, always prioritizing safety and efficacy.

### Why Diffusion Models Use Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)
**Classifier-free guidance** is a technique used in diffusion models (e.g., DALL·E 2, Stable Diffusion) to **enhance control over generated outputs** (e.g., aligning images with text prompts) without relying on an external classifier. Here’s why it’s widely adopted:

1. **Stronger Prompt Adherence**:  
   CFG amplifies the influence of conditional inputs (e.g., text prompts) by comparing a **"conditional"** prediction (guided by the prompt) with an **"unconditional"** prediction (no prompt). The difference between these is scaled and added to the final output, making generations more faithful to the prompt.

2. **Avoids Classifier Limitations**:  
   Earlier methods like **classifier guidance** required training a separate classifier to steer diffusion. This was brittle—classifiers struggled with noisy data, added computational overhead, and limited flexibility for diverse conditions (e.g., complex text).

3. **Simplicity & Efficiency**:  
   CFG trains a **single model** to handle both conditional and unconditional` generation by randomly dropping prompts during training (e.g., 10–20% of the time). At inference, it combines both pathways, avoiding extra models or complex setups.

---

### Why Is CFG Considered a "Hack"?
Despite its effectiveness, CFG is often called a "hack" for these reasons:
1. **Distribution Mismatch**:  
   CFG artificially exaggerates the difference between conditional and unconditional outputs. This pushes samples away from the true data distribution, leading to artifacts (e.g., oversaturated colors, unrealistic details).

2. **Hyperparameter Sensitivity**:  
   The **guidance scale** (e.g., `scale=7.0` in Stable Diffusion) must be tuned carefully. High values improve prompt alignment but reduce diversity/image quality; low values weaken control.

3. **Theoretical Impropriety**:  
   CFG isn’t derived from probabilistic principles. It’s an empirical trick that "hijacks" the model’s training objective, making generations **less probabilistic** and more deterministic.

4. **Trade-Offs**:  
   It sacrifices sample diversity for controllability—a compromise not inherent to the diffusion process itself.

---

### Better Alternatives to CFG
While CFG remains popular, these alternatives aim for more principled control:

1. **Reinforcement Learning (RL) Fine-Tuning**:  
   - **How**: Use RL (e.g., PPO) to optimize diffusion model outputs for reward metrics (e.g., prompt-image alignment via CLIP).  
   - **Pros**: Directly optimizes for desired objectives; avoids distribution distortion.  
   - **Cons**: Computationally expensive; unstable training.  
   - **Example**: [DPOK](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13301) integrates RL with diffusion.

2. **GAN-Based Steering**:  
   - **How**: Employ a GAN discriminator to guide diffusion sampling toward high-reward regions.  
   - **Pros**: Leverages adversarial training for finer control.  
   - **Cons**: Adds complexity; GAN training challenges remain.  
   - **Example**: [Guided-Diffusion+GAN hybrids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12647).

3. **Improved Sampling Techniques**:  
   - **Consistency Models**: Train models to map noise to data in fewer steps, reducing the need for guidance.  
   - **Rectified Flow**: Straightens sampling trajectories for more efficient/stable generation.  
   - **Pros**: Faster sampling; less guidance dependency.

4. **Architectural Enhancements**:  
   - **Cross-Attention Refinement**: Strengthen text-image alignment in the model architecture (e.g., deeper cross-attention layers).  
   - **Perceiver Resamplers**: Better compress conditional inputs (e.g., long text) for more precise control.

5. **Energy-Based Models (EBMs)**:  
   - **How**: Use EBMs to define a scoring function for desired attributes, guiding diffusion sampling.  
   - **Pros**: Theoretically grounded; flexible control.

### Why Diffusion Models Use Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)
**Classifier-free guidance** is a technique used in diffusion models (e.g., DALL·E 2, Stable Diffusion) to **enhance control over generated outputs** (e.g., aligning images with text prompts) without relying on an external classifier. Here’s why it’s widely adopted:

1. **Stronger Prompt Adherence**:  
   CFG amplifies the influence of conditional inputs (e.g., text prompts) by comparing a **"conditional"** prediction (guided by the prompt) with an **"unconditional"** prediction (no prompt). The difference between these is scaled and added to the final output, making generations more faithful to the prompt.

2. **Avoids Classifier Limitations**:  
   Earlier methods like **classifier guidance** required training a separate classifier to steer diffusion. This was brittle—classifiers struggled with noisy data, added computational overhead, and limited flexibility for diverse conditions (e.g., complex text).

3. **Simplicity & Efficiency**:  
   CFG trains a **single model** to handle both conditional and unconditional` generation by randomly dropping prompts during training (e.g., 10–20% of the time). At inference, it combines both pathways, avoiding extra models or complex setups.

---

### Why Is CFG Considered a "Hack"?
Despite its effectiveness, CFG is often called a "hack" for these reasons:
1. **Distribution Mismatch**:  
   CFG artificially exaggerates the difference between conditional and unconditional outputs. This pushes samples away from the true data distribution, leading to artifacts (e.g., oversaturated colors, unrealistic details).

2. **Hyperparameter Sensitivity**:  
   The **guidance scale** (e.g., `scale=7.0` in Stable Diffusion) must be tuned carefully. High values improve prompt alignment but reduce diversity/image quality; low values weaken control.

3. **Theoretical Impropriety**:  
   CFG isn’t derived from probabilistic principles. It’s an empirical trick that "hijacks" the model’s training objective, making generations **less probabilistic** and more deterministic.

4. **Trade-Offs**:  
   It sacrifices sample diversity for controllability—a compromise not inherent to the diffusion process itself.

---

### Better Alternatives to CFG
While CFG remains popular, these alternatives aim for more principled control:

1. **Reinforcement Learning (RL) Fine-Tuning**:  
   - **How**: Use RL (e.g., PPO) to optimize diffusion model outputs for reward metrics (e.g., prompt-image alignment via CLIP).  
   - **Pros**: Directly optimizes for desired objectives; avoids distribution distortion.  
   - **Cons**: Computationally expensive; unstable training.  
   - **Example**: [DPOK](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13301) integrates RL with diffusion.

2. **GAN-Based Steering**:  
   - **How**: Employ a GAN discriminator to guide diffusion sampling toward high-reward regions.  
   - **Pros**: Leverages adversarial training for finer control.  
   - **Cons**: Adds complexity; GAN training challenges remain.  
   - **Example**: [Guided-Diffusion+GAN hybrids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12647).

3. **Improved Sampling Techniques**:  
   - **Consistency Models**: Train models to map noise to data in fewer steps, reducing the need for guidance.  
   - **Rectified Flow**: Straightens sampling trajectories for more efficient/stable generation.  
   - **Pros**: Faster sampling; less guidance dependency.

4. **Architectural Enhancements**:  
   - **Cross-Attention Refinement**: Strengthen text-image alignment in the model architecture (e.g., deeper cross-attention layers).  
   - **Perceiver Resamplers**: Better compress conditional inputs (e.g., long text) for more precise control.

5. **Energy-Based Models (EBMs)**:  
   - **How**: Use EBMs to define a scoring function for desired attributes, guiding diffusion sampling.  
   - **Pros**: Theoretically grounded; flexible control.  
   - **Cons**: Sampling slow; training instability.

---

### Key Insight
CFG dominates because it’s **simple, effective, and lightweight**—but its empirical nature and trade-offs make it a pragmatic "hack." Alternatives like RL or architectural innovations offer more rigor but at higher computational cost. As diffusion models evolve, expect hybrid approaches (e.g., CFG + RL) to bridge practicality and theory. For now, CFG remains the go-to for most applications.
